direct_claims: This chart shows the share of British adults who smoke cigarettes or use vapes/e-cigarettes over time.
The subject belongs to public health and tobacco control.
The chart was published by Our World in Data.
The cited data sources are the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and Action on Smoking and Health (ASH).
The note states that cigarette use is measured for adults aged 16 and older, while vaping is measured for adults aged 18 and older.
The note also states that any vaping use is included, including occasional use.
The cigarette and vaping lines are shown as separate prevalence series rather than as parts of a single total.
The chart does not provide exact annual values in a table, confidence intervals, or methodological detail beyond the short note and source citation.
Because the image alone is being used, some numeric statements here are approximate rather than exact.
derived_claims: The smoking series begins in the mid-1970s at roughly 45% and falls to about 10% by 2023. — derived by reading approximate start and end values from the smoking line and y-axis.
The vaping series appears only in the 2010s and rises from around 2% to about 9% by 2023. — derived by reading approximate start and end values from the vaping line and y-axis.

Because the age thresholds differ between the two series, the smoking and vaping percentages are not perfectly like-for-like measures. — derived by comparing the note about age definitions across the two series.
The chart does not show whether people who vape are former smokers, current smokers, or people who use both products. — derived from the absence of subgroup breakdowns in the chart image.

The long-term fall in smoking suggests substantial public-health gains relative to the much higher smoking levels seen in the 1970s. — derived by comparing approximate smoking prevalence in the 1970s with 2023.
The rise in vaping suggests that nicotine use behavior is changing rather than simply disappearing. — derived by comparing downward smoking trend with upward vaping trend.

The differing age definitions in the note are important for decision-making because they can affect direct comparisons between smoking and vaping prevalence. — derived by interpreting the methodological note about age thresholds.
speculative_claims: The chart’s purpose is likely to show how nicotine consumption patterns in Britain have shifted away from combustible cigarettes and toward vaping over time. — source: public health data communication.

In tobacco-control terms, cigarette smoking and vaping are related but not identical behaviors, because smoking involves combustible tobacco while vaping typically involves inhaled aerosol from e-cigarette devices. — source: tobacco control and public health.
A drop in smoking prevalence usually indicates fewer adults are exposed to the well-established health risks of combustible tobacco use. — source: epidemiology and public health.

That distinction matters because, in this field, vaping can be interpreted differently depending on whether it reflects smoking cessation, dual use, or new nicotine uptake. — source: tobacco control research.
The chart matters because smoking prevalence has a major relationship to disease burden, mortality, and healthcare costs. — source: public health and health economics.
Policymakers, health services, smoking-cessation programs, and regulators are all affected by this kind of trend data. — source: health policy and regulation.
If smoking continues to decline, Britain could see further reductions in smoking-related illness over time. — source: epidemiology and public health.

If vaping continues to rise, public debate may increasingly focus on balancing harm reduction for smokers against concerns about nicotine dependence and uptake among non-smokers. — source: tobacco policy.
